title: Care for, select and use hand and measuring tools

lessons.title: Knowing your hand tools
lessons.html:
Hand tools in the workshop

Hand tools are tools you use with your own strength, not with electricity or air. In a farm workshop you use them every day to fix tractors, trailers and implements.

Common hand tools

ToolWhat it is for
Spanners (open and ring)Turning nuts and bolts
Socket set with ratchetTurning nuts and bolts quickly
Screwdrivers (flat and Phillips)Turning screws
PliersHolding, bending and cutting wire
HammerHitting, such as driving a pin
HacksawCutting metal
FileSmoothing rough metal edges
Chisel and punchCutting metal, marking centres, driving out pins
Allen keysTurning bolts with a six-sided hole

Choose the right tool

  • Use a spanner that fits the nut exactly. A loose spanner slips and rounds the corners of the nut, and you can hurt your hand.
  • Use the correct type and size of screwdriver for the screw head.
  • Ring spanners and sockets grip better than open spanners.
  • Never use a screwdriver as a chisel or a spanner as a hammer.
  • Never put a pipe on a spanner to make it longer. It can break or slip.

Check before you use

  • Is the handle tight and not cracked?
  • Is the hammer head firmly on the handle?
  • Are the jaws of the spanner worn or spread?
  • Does the chisel have a mushroom head (spread, cracked top)? This can throw chips into your eyes. Give it in to be fixed.

If a tool is damaged, do not use it. Tell your supervisor.

lessons.title: Measuring tools and how to use them
lessons.html:
Measuring in the workshop

We measure to cut metal to the right length, to check that parts fit, and to set gaps correctly.

Common measuring tools

  • Steel rule: a flat metal ruler marked in millimetres (mm) and centimetres (cm).
  • Measuring tape: for long lengths, such as a trailer frame.
  • Try square: checks that a corner is square (90 degrees).
  • Vernier caliper: measures small sizes accurately, such as the thickness of a bolt.
  • Feeler gauges: thin metal blades to measure small gaps.
  • Tyre pressure gauge: checks air in tyres.

Units

10 mm = 1 cm. 100 cm = 1 m. 1 000 mm = 1 m. Most workshop measurements are in millimetres.

Using a steel rule or tape

  1. Clean the part.
  2. Put the zero end exactly at the start of the part.
  3. Keep the rule straight along the part.
  4. Look straight down at the marks, not from the side.
  5. Read the number and write it down with the unit, such as 450 mm.

Marking out

After measuring, mark the metal with a scriber or marker. Use the try square to draw a straight line across. Measure twice before you cut once.

Using a try square

Hold the thick part (the stock) against one edge. Look at the blade against the other edge. If there is a gap, the corner is not square.

Using feeler gauges

Choose the blade with the size you need. Slide it into the gap. It should slide in with a light drag. Ask your mentor to show you the right feel.

lessons.title: Using tools safely and looking after them
lessons.html:
Working safely with tools

  • Wear safety glasses when hammering, chiselling, filing or cutting.
  • Wear gloves when handling sharp or rough metal.
  • Pull a spanner towards you rather than pushing it, so you do not hit your knuckles if it slips.
  • Hold work in a vice when cutting or filing.
  • Keep your hands behind the cutting edge of a chisel or file.
  • Use a file with a handle. A bare file tang can stab your hand.
  • Do not carry sharp tools in your pockets.
  • Keep your work area tidy so you do not trip over tools.

Using a hacksaw

  1. Fit the blade with the teeth pointing forward, away from the handle.
  2. Clamp the metal in the vice, close to the cut.
  3. Use long, steady strokes. Press on the forward stroke and lift slightly on the back stroke.
  4. Slow down at the end of the cut so the piece does not fall onto your foot.

Cleaning tools

  • Wipe off oil, grease and dirt after use.
  • Put a light coat of oil on steel tools to stop rust.
  • Clean files with a file card (a wire brush for files).

Storing tools

  • Put every tool back in its place in the toolbox or on the tool board.
  • Keep measuring tools in their boxes, away from heavy tools.
  • Never drop measuring tools. They can become wrong.
  • Count your tools at the end of the job. A spanner left inside a machine can cause damage.

Reporting

Report broken, worn or missing tools to your supervisor. Do not hide damage.

Key points

  • Choose the right tool and the right size for the job.
  • Check tools for damage before use and never use a damaged tool.
  • Wear safety glasses and keep work in a vice.
  • Measure carefully: start at zero, look straight down, write the unit.
  • Measure twice, cut once.
  • Clean, oil and put tools back in their place; count them after a job.
